amendments.rule: **A numeral phrase may hold more waws than the ASV renders.** Align the ASV's *and* to the waw standing between the same two numerals the English *and* stands between, and mark any other waw in the phrase `unrepresented`. In `חָמֵשׁ וְתִשְׁעִים שָׁנָה וּשְׁמֹנֶה מֵאוֹת שָׁנָה` → *eight hundred ninety and five years* the English *and* joins ninety to five, so the units-to-tens waw takes it and the waw at the group boundary has nothing; in `תְּשַׁע מֵאוֹת שָׁנָה וּשְׁלֹשִׁים שָׁנָה` → *nine hundred and thirty years* the same English *and* joins the two groups, so there the group-boundary waw is the one that takes it. This is determined rather than a tie-break: the ASV's *and* stands between specific numerals, so read which, rather than preferring a position. **The surplus runs the other way just as often.** Where the phrase holds more English *and*s than waws, an *and* standing between two numerals no waw joins is `added` under rule 30, because no morpheme licenses it: `מֵאָה שְׁנֵים עָשָׂר` → *a hundred and twelve*, `אֶלֶף שִׁבְעָה עָשָׂר` → *a thousand and seventeen*, `שְׁמֹנֶה מֵאוֹת שְׁמֹנָה עָשָׂר` → *eight hundred and eighteen*, `אַרְבַּע רִבּוֹא אַלְפַּיִם` → *forty and two thousand*. Do not fold such an *and* into a neighbouring numeral's unit to avoid the `added`: rule 30's fusion wants one English word, and this *and* is written beside the numerals rather than inside one of them. Count the waws, count the *and*s, and set them against each other by the pair of numerals each stands between; whichever side is in surplus is what the two halves of this rule dispose of. An ASV italic on such an *and* corroborates it, and the absence of one is not evidence against it, by rule 7. **But the numerals the count runs between are the ones the Hebrew writes, not the ones the English writes.** Where a single Hebrew numeral is rendered by a fixed English compound that contains an *and* of its own — `שִׁבְעִים` → *threescore and ten* — that word coordinates the parts of one morpheme's rendering rather than two source items, so it joins that numeral's unit under rule 14's closing sentence, is neither `added` nor any waw's, and does not move the unit's head. Decide it by the subtraction test rules 14, 16 and 31 use: ask what stands on either side of the English *and* in the Hebrew. Where a source numeral stands on each side, the sentences above govern and the surplus is marked; where the same one numeral's rendering runs on both sides, no source item is coordinated at all and there is nothing to mark. One list may write both, and 2CH.29.32 does: `שִׁבְעִים בָּקָר` → *threescore and ten bullocks* keeps its *and* inside the numeral's unit, while the *and* of *a hundred rams and two hundred lambs* stands between two numerals the Hebrew writes separately with no waw between them and is `added`.
amendments.why: Rule 42's `added` clause says *two numerals* without saying whose, and its counting instruction can be read off the English. 2CH.29.32 writes both cases in one list, and a literal count of that verse — zero waws in the numeral run against two English *and*s — would strip the *and* out of `שִׁבְעִים` → *threescore and ten* as a surplus. Rule 14's closing sentence already decides it the other way for a source morpheme generally, and the verse pass reached the right answer only by going there, so the amendment narrows an over-broad sentence rather than adding new law, and cannot conflict with precedent aligned under rule 14. It is placed in rule 42 because that is the rule a numeral phrase sends a verse pass to, and genealogies and censuses are where scored numerals like *threescore and ten* and *fourscore and ten* recur. No corpus row for `שֶׁבַע` → *threescore and ten* was in the packet; the amendment does not rest on one.

conventions: `עַד` + `לְ` is read by what the `לְ` governs. Before a noun, where the ASV writes a single English word for the pair, the two fuse under rule 30 and the unit heads on `עַד`: `עַד־לְשִׂמְחָה` → *with* (29.30 s025+s026). Before an infinitive construct the `לְ` is that verb's own marker and not half of a compound preposition, so `עַד` takes the written *until* or *till* by itself and the `לְ` is `unrepresented` under rules 40 and 52: `עַד לִכְלוֹת הָעֹלָה` → *until the burnt offering was finished* (29.28 s016, s017), aligned exactly as the `לְ`-less `עַד־כְּלוֹת הַמְּלָאכָה` → *till the work was ended* (29.34 s023) is. Both units name the competing rule 30 fusion in their notes; the chapter took the split, and the corpus was not consulted for `עַד לְ` before an infinitive.

`פְּנִימָה` takes only what the ASV writes for it, and the discriminator is whether that rendering is already complete without the supplied words. At 29.16 the adverb's whole rendering is the phrase *the inner part*, which joins its unit under rule 31 headed on *inner*, since dropping *part* leaves no rendering of the lexeme. At 29.18 the ASV writes a complete *within* for the adverb and then supplies an italic *the palace* — both the determiner and a head noun the Hebrew never writes — which is its own `added` unit under rule 33's supplied-head-noun case. Do not fold that noun phrase into the adverb on the strength of the 29.16 unit.

report: Checked all 74 candidate lemma groups and read the dump end to end for the splits the table cannot show (the 15 `added` units). No construction is analysed two ways with nothing in the source licensing the difference, so no patches.

Supplied connectives and complementizers are counted rather than folded in every verse that has one: 2CH.29.18 t022 (three waws against four English connectives; the surplus stands before the asyndetic object marker, while s019/s024/s029 take the two *with*s and the *and* written for them), 2CH.29.27 t023 (*also* in a clause with no waw, rule 51), 2CH.29.32 t020 (rule 42) and 2CH.29.24 t028 (rule 55). Nothing elsewhere in the chapter absorbs a supplied connective into a neighbouring morpheme to avoid an `added`.

Rule 29's three cases are each decided by reading which word the written *the* stands before: fronted onto an anarthrously rendered rectum (29.18 s017, s027), arthrous rectum with a supplied *the* on the construct (29.7, 12, 15, 20, 23, 32, 35), and the English possessive *the king's seer* (29.25 s021). Agreement and vocative articles go `unrepresented` under rules 47 and 36 (29.3, 29.5, 29.17). Consistent in all 97 article units.

Two constructions were handled two ways, and in both the source licenses the difference, so they are logged as conventions rather than patched: `עַד` + `לְ` (fused before a noun at 29.30, split before an infinitive construct at 29.28) and `פְּנִימָה` (a whole multi-word rendering at 29.16, a complete *within* beside a supplied `added` noun phrase at 29.18). Both pairs already name the competing reading in their unit notes, as rule 8 requires.

Also verified internally consistent: the single aligned object marker of 22 (29.24 s008, the role-phrase *with*; the other 21 stand on objects the ASV writes bare); the comparative `מִן` taking both *more* and *than* at 29.34; supplied possessives `added` at 29.6 t036 and 29.30 t035 under rule 18's closing sentence; the three directive-`he` altars of 29.22/24 taking their own *on* or *upon* while 29.16's `חוּצָה` fuses for the single word *abroad*; and every `עֹלָה` headed on *burnt*.

BSB: all 16 disagreements are documented convention differences, and none is a genuine error. The seven Td cases are agreement articles (29.3 s005/s013, 29.17 s008/s039), a vocative article (29.5 s007) and articles the ASV writes no *the* for at all (29.19 s008 *king Ahaz*, 29.36 s011 *God*). The five R cases are recastings that leave the preposition nothing to say (29.8 s017, the third of three `לְ`s against two written *to be*s; 29.11 s007, 29.21 s029 and 29.30 s009, all bare English objects after a verb; 29.34 s010, a bare infinitive after *could not*). The two `אֵת` cases and 29.27 s023 and 29.30 s009 are the same two conventions again. Do not change any of these to raise the 98.1%.

One data note for a later reader: 29.26 s011 `בַּ` is tagged `Rd` but MACULA supplies no `Td` token beside it, so the ASV's *the* before *trumpets* is necessarily supplied and joins the noun. That is forced by the token partition rather than a judgment, and it is why that phrase looks unlike the six `Rd` + `[הַ]` pairs elsewhere in the chapter.
